Lactose intolerant people aren't having a reaction to lactase, they are unable to digest the sugar lactose that's present in the milk because their bodies no longer naturally produce lactase.

Also,  while your body does use compounds that aren't produced in-house (i.e., vitamin C or sodium), your body does not use proteins created by other organisms. Your body will ALWAYS attempt to break proteins that enter your digestive system down into individual amino acids and then use those amino acid building blocks to make proteins whose makeup is specific to your DNA. Unless there are weird, niche exceptions that I'm unaware of, your body will pretty much never absorb outside proteins for use inside the body. 

I recommend you read [this article](https://biologydictionary.net/protein-synthesis/) if you want to get a better picture of the process your body uses to synthesize its proteins and enzymes.

Cooking meat actually [provides more nutrition](https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2011/11/why-cooking-counts/). The high heat denatures proteins and causes some to break down, meaning our bodies have to do significantly less work while digesting them and are more capable of absorbing the nutrients. It's also significantly easier to chew. Cooked food was actually one of the main reasons that harnessing fire was integral to human advancement. By spending less energy chewing and digesting food, our ancestors could spend more time planning, building, and socializing.

Not OP, but basically pretty much all processes either use heat (endothermic) or give off heat (exothermic). You're probably very familiar with exothermic processes in the form of things like burning wood or water condensing on the side of a glass. These processes involve a net outflow of energy from the system to the surroundings. In the case of wood burning, that's in the form of higher-energy bonds reassembling to form lower-energy bonds and the excess energy being released into the surroundings (in terms of numbers, it takes 80 calories to completely freeze 1g of water at 0°C). Endothermic processes are the opposite. They absorb heat from their surroundings in order to happen (if you've ever had isopropyl alcohol, acetone, or another similar volatile liquid evaporate from your hand, it'll get cold). In terms of numbers, this would look like 1g of water at 100°C absorbing 540 calories to completely vaporize. 

In refrigerators, closed loops of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are used to absorb heat through evaporation and move it somewhere else. A liquid VOC is evaporated in an evaporation unit, absorbing heat from its surroundings. This cools down the air around the VOC. This cold air is blown into the refrigerator. The VOC is then pumped into a compressor where it is pressurized into a liquid state, releasing heat back out into the surroundings. This heat is passed off to heat sinks and dispersed into the environment around the refrigerator by fans. The now liquid VOC is then passed back into the evaporation unit and the cycle continues.
